title: The Lion and Sun: an emblem and its changing uses
standfirst: A solar lion appears on coins, metalwork, tiles and flags. What do we know about where it comes from?
seoTitle: The Lion and Sun: history of an Iranian emblem
metaDescription: A sourced introduction to the Persian Lion and Sun emblem: its astrological roots, its long use on objects, and its place on Iran's flag until 1979.

body.text: The lion-and-sun motif combines a lion with the sun, and was a central element of Iran's national flag until 1979 [@wp-lionsun]. It appears widely on coins, metalwork, tiles and miniature paintings across Iran, Central Asia and India [@wp-lionsun].

Writers connect the motif to the astrological association of the sun with the sign of Leo, an idea some trace to ancient West Asian traditions linking sun gods and lions [@wp-lionsun]. A version with the sun half-hidden behind a lion appears in a fourteenth-century manuscript of Albumasar's *Book of Nativities*, illustrated by Qanbar ʿAli Shirazi [@wp-lionsun]. Evidence for earlier forms is debated, and the motif became widely popular from the twelfth century [@wp-lionsun]. [VERIFY with a tier A source before publication.]

The scholar Afsaneh Najmabadi has argued that the emblem has had "a unique success" as a sign of modern Iranian identity because it draws on several traditions, among them Zoroastrian, Shia and Jewish symbolism [@wp-lionsun; @najmabadi2005]. [VERIFY quotation and page in Najmabadi before publication; second-hand at present.]
The emblem remains in use in different contexts. Because it is politically contested, this archive describes designs and sources and does not endorse any current use of the symbol.
